Chapter 16.4

How do medical advancements impact human reproduction and survival?

Infections that travel, medicines that work on some of them, and a population that grew.

Two patients take the same tablet. One recovers and one does not. What is different about what made them ill?

What you will be able to do by the end

  • State how sexually transmitted infections are passed on, including the routes that are not sexual intercourse.
  • State the harmful long-term effects of syphilis, gonorrhoea and HIV.
  • State what antibiotics do to bacteria.
  • Explain why bacterial infections can be cured by antibiotics but viral ones cannot.
  • State how the transmission of these infections can be prevented.
  • Suggest reasons for the world’s growing human population.

Where does an infection get into this system?

  • Something other than sperm can travel the same route. Where does it get in?
  • Sexually transmitted infections are mainly passed on during sexual intercourse, so they enter along the same tract map you already know.The same path a sperm takes is a path an infection can take. That is why the barrier that stops one also stops the other.
  • A transmission route is any way an infection gets from one person to another.Transmission means passing an infection from one person to another.
  • Not every route runs through this system. Some do not involve sexual intercourse at all.A person can catch one of these without ever having sex. That is why the next slide matters even to someone who thinks it cannot apply to them.
  • Sexual intercourse is the main route, but it is not the only one.
  • A condom used correctly and consistently blocks the main route.
  • It may not be completely effective.

Why does a condom reduce the spread of these infections as well as preventing pregnancy?

How else can these infections pass from person to person?

  • Three other routes exist. Can you think of one before you read on?
  • Sexually transmitted infections are diseases related to the human reproductive system. They are mainly transmitted during sexual intercourse.Sexually transmitted infection is a disease passed on mainly during sexual intercourse. It is often shortened to STI.
  • Some may also be transmitted through blood transfusion, or through sharing of unsterilised or contaminated needles.A needle that has been inside one person and is then used on another carries whatever was in the first person’s blood. That is why injections, piercings and tattoos all matter here.
  • They may also pass from a mother to infant during childbirth or breast-feeding.The baby is not infected by anything it did. It receives the infection from its mother during birth or feeding.
  • Needles matter for injections, body piercings and tattooing alike.
  • A baby can be infected without any sexual contact at all.
  • Knowing all four routes is what the objective asks for.

What do these three infections actually do to a person?

  • Three named infections. Which of their effects last a lifetime?
  • Syphilis causes painless sores and red rashes, fever, headache and fatigue. Long term it can cause blindness, paralysis, major brain and heart damage, and infertility.Painless is the dangerous word here. A sore that does not hurt is easy to ignore, so the infection can be passed on for a long time.Infertility is the inability to conceive: the reproductive system can no longer start a pregnancy.
  • Gonorrhoea causes a burning sensation during urination, a discharge of pus, and pain in the lower abdomen. Long term it can cause infertility and lasting pelvic or abdominal pain.Pus is the thick yellow liquid formed in infected body tissue. Its appearance is often the first sign a person notices.
  • Human immunodeficiency virus causes flu-like symptoms, usually in the later stages. Untreated it develops into acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, a weakened immune system, and death.
  • Two of these three are bacterial and one is viral.
  • Two of the three can cause infertility.
  • The flu-like symptoms of the viral one appear late, so a person can pass it on without knowing.

The situation

Two patients are seen on the same morning.

One has an infection caused by bacteria. The other has an infection caused by a virus.

Both are given exactly the same tablet, at the same dose, for the same number of days.

What happens next: Neither patient takes anything else, and neither changes anything about their daily life.

Decide, before you read on: what happens to each patient? Then say what would have to be true about that tablet for both to get better.

Last slide You predicted that one patient recovers and one does not.This slide asks So what is different about the two things making them ill?

What is a bacterium made of, and what is a virus made of?

  • One of these is built like every other living thing. Which one?
  • A bacterium is a living cell. It has a cell wall, a cell membrane, cytoplasm and its own genetic material, and it grows and divides on its own.Bacterium is a single living cell. Living cell means it has the parts a cell has and can grow and divide by itself. Genetic material is the set of instructions for building and running whatever it sits inside.
  • A virus is not a cell. It is genetic material inside a protein coat, and it cannot grow or divide on its own.A virus has no cell wall, no membrane of its own and no cytoplasm. It is a set of instructions in a case, and it needs to get inside one of your cells to do anything at all.
  • That single difference decides which medicines can work.Everything on the next slide follows from this one fact. If you remember nothing else, remember that one of them is a cell and the other is not.
  • A bacterium is a living cell; a virus is not.
  • Syphilis and gonorrhoea are bacterial. HIV is viral.
  • This is the fact every question about curing them depends on.

Which statement is true of a virus but not of a bacterium?

Last slide A bacterium is a living cell and a virus is not.This slide asks So what does that leave a medicine to work on?

What can a medicine attack if there is no cell to attack?

  • If the medicine attacks parts of a cell, what happens when there is no cell?
  • An antibiotic can kill harmful bacteria or stop their growth.Antibiotic is a medicine that kills bacteria or stops them growing. It does nothing to a virus.
  • So antibiotics can be used to treat diseases caused by bacteria, such as syphilis and gonorrhoea.Both of those are caused by bacteria, and bacteria are living cells. The medicine has real parts to act on, so the patient recovers.
  • Antibiotics have no effect on diseases transmitted by viruses, such as HIV and influenza.The antibiotic goes looking for the parts a bacterial cell has. A virus does not have them. The medicine finds nothing to act on, and the patient does not get better.
  • Antibiotics kill bacteria or stop their growth.
  • Some bacterial infections can be cured by antibiotics, but viral ones cannot.
  • Influenza is viral, which is why antibiotics do not cure a flu.

Last slide Curing one person is not the same as stopping the next case.This slide asks So what stops transmission in the first place?

How can these infections be stopped from spreading at all?

  • Curing someone happens after the fact. What stops it happening at all?
  • The transmission of these infections can be prevented by using condoms correctly and consistently.Consistently means every single time, not just sometimes. Using one most times still leaves the route open.
  • However, this may not be completely effective.Completely effective would mean the risk drops to zero. It does not. It drops a long way, which is worth a great deal, but it is not the same as none.
  • The best way to avoid transmitting or contracting these infections is by practising abstinence.Abstinence means not having sex at all.
  • Correctly and consistently are both required; one without the other is not enough.
  • Antibiotics treat two of these three, but treatment is not prevention.
  • A vaccine protects against some diseases, but there is no cure for the viral one here.

Why is "used consistently" part of the statement about condoms?

Last slide Medicine can now cure infections that used to kill.This slide asks So what did that do to the number of people alive?

Why did the number of people on Earth rise so steeply?

  • Four different advances all pushed the same number up. What were they?
  • New drugs, vaccines and advanced medical treatments helped people survive and live longer lives, so the world population grew greatly.A vaccine protects a person from a disease before they ever meet it. Fewer people dying young means more people alive at any one moment.
  • A vaccine protected people against deadly diseases such as smallpox and tuberculosis.
  • Improved food production, transportation and sanitation all did the same thing from a different direction.Sanitation means clean water and safe disposal of human waste, so diseases like cholera and typhoid do not spread.
  • Better sanitation reduced the spread of cholera and typhoid.
  • Better food production meant fewer people died of hunger.
  • Better transport moved food and medicines to more places, faster.

How did improved sanitation raise the number of people alive?

2.Vaccine: the person meets the disease but is protected
3.Antibiotic: the person is ill and is then cured
4.Lung machine: the person is already dying and is kept alive

Six questions, one for each thing you learnt

Check yourself0 / 6

  1. Which of these is a way these infections spread that does not involve sexual intercourse?

    Sharing unsterilised or contaminated needles is one of the routes, along with blood transfusion and mother to infant.

  2. Which long-term effect is listed for both syphilis and gonorrhoea?

    Both list infertility. Blindness is syphilis only; a weakened immune system follows the viral infection.

  3. What do antibiotics do?

    Antibiotics can kill harmful bacteria or stop their growth. They do nothing to viruses.

  4. Why can antibiotics not cure HIV?

    A bacterium is a living cell with parts an antibiotic acts on. A virus is genetic material in a protein coat, and has none of them.

  5. What is described as the best way to avoid these infections?

    Condoms used correctly and consistently prevent transmission but may not be completely effective. Abstinence is described as the best way.

  6. Which of these helped the world population grow?

    Vaccines, better food production, better transport and better sanitation all helped more people survive and live longer.

Three things worth knowing0 / 3
Tap a card to turn it over.
1Alexander Fleming found a dish contaminated with a fungus. What had happened around it?The fungus had killed the bacteria he was growing.
2What did he do instead of calling it a failed experiment?He asked what in the fungus could kill bacteria. That substance was penicillin.
3What does a clinical research manager do?Makes sure clinical trials on new medicines are run fairly, so a product is effective and safe before it is sold.
